content.summary: Toasting an ingredient in a dry hot pan with no fat until aromatic and lightly coloured.
content.how_to: Heat a pan on medium, add the dal or spice, stir constantly until it turns a shade darker and smells nutty (2-4 minutes). Remove immediately so it does not scorch.
content.sensory_cues: Nutty aroma; moong dal turns pale gold; no smoke.
content.failure_modes: Burning at high heat gives a bitter taste; under-roasting gives no aroma benefit.

content.summary: Leaving a ground rice-and-dal batter at warm room temperature so wild lactic-acid bacteria and yeast raise it and sour it.
content.how_to: Mix the ground rice and dal with salt, cover loosely, keep somewhere warm (around 25-30 C) for 8-16 hours until the batter has roughly doubled and smells pleasantly sour with visible bubbles.
content.sensory_cues: Volume more than doubled; domed, bubbly surface; clean sour smell.
content.failure_modes: Too cold or too short: flat batter, no rise, dense idli. Too long or too warm: over-sour, thin batter.

content.summary: Heating a thin liquid dish only until it foams up at the edges, then taking it off - never letting it roll to a hard boil, which would turn it bitter and cloudy.
content.how_to: Keep the heat low to medium; watch for a white froth rising up the sides and the surface just trembling, then switch off. For rasam this is the moment the raw smell of the tamarind and spice powder disappears.
content.sensory_cues: A ring of froth climbs the pan; the liquid is aromatic, not raw-smelling; no violent bubbling.
content.failure_modes: Hard boiling: bitter, muddy, the fresh aroma is cooked off.

content.summary: Cooking under sealed steam pressure to soften grains and pulses quickly.
content.how_to: Combine rice, dal and water in the cooker, close, cook on medium for 3-4 whistles, then let the pressure fall naturally before opening.
content.sensory_cues: Grains fully collapsed and mashable; mixture pourable while hot.
content.failure_modes: Too little water or a fast pressure release gives a stiff, dry mass.

content.summary: Cooking food in the vapour above simmering water, in a covered vessel, so it cooks gently without browning or drying.
content.how_to: Bring an inch of water to the boil in a steamer or a wide pot with a trivet, set the filled moulds or plate above the water line, cover, and steam on medium.
content.sensory_cues: For idli: a skewer comes out clean after about 10 minutes; the cake springs back when pressed.
content.failure_modes: Water touching the food: soggy result. Lid not tight: long cooking, dense texture.

content.summary: Blooming whole spices and aromatics in hot fat, then pouring the fragrant fat over the finished dish.
content.how_to: Heat ghee or oil until shimmering, add spices in order of cooking time (cumin and pepper first, then cashew, then curry leaves and asafoetida), fry a few seconds until they crackle and colour, pour over the dish.
content.sensory_cues: Cumin sizzles and darkens; curry leaves go crisp and translucent; strong aroma.
content.failure_modes: Fat not hot enough: spices go soggy, no aroma. Fat too hot: spices burn and turn bitter.

content.summary: Grinding soaked grains or pulses with a little water into a smooth, aerated paste, traditionally in a stone wet grinder.
content.how_to: Drain the soaked ingredient, grind in short bursts adding cold water a splash at a time, until the paste is smooth and light; grind urad dal fine and fluffy, rice a little coarse.
content.sensory_cues: Urad paste is white, smooth and holds a soft peak; a drop floats in water.
content.failure_modes: Too much water or over-grinding rice: thin batter, flat idli.
